messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] potential bug in predict(fm, "det"...) when appendData=T
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] potential bug in predict(fm, "det"...) when appendData=T
messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard,

Here's a short reproducible example, with some long-winded observations...

################################################################################

library(unmarked)
set.seed(81)

# Simulated double-observer survey data
i= 1:100                 # Site index, 100 sites total
Ni= rep(c(2,5), 50)      # True abundance at sites, mean lambda alternating between 2 and 5

HabType= rep(c("A","B"), 50) # Habitat type that abundance depends on.

p1= 0.80                 # Detection probability of first observer ("Billy")
p2= 0.95                 # Detection probability of second observer ("Bob")

Name1= rep("Billy", 100) # Name of first observer
Name2= rep("Bob", 100)   # Name of second observer

## Observation-level covariates ------------------------------------------------
obsCovs= list( Observer= cbind(Name1, Name2) )

## Counts ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Count1= rbinom(length(i), Ni, p1)  # Billy's counts
Count2= rbinom(length(i), Ni, p2)  # Bob's counts
y= cbind(Count1, Count2) # response formatted for umf

## Site-level covariates -------------------------------------------------------
siteCovs= data.frame( i= i,
                      HabType= as.factor(HabType))

## Construct the unmarked frame ------------------------------------------------
umf1= unmarkedFramePCount(y=y, siteCovs=siteCovs, obsCovs=obsCovs)

(obsCovs(umf1)$Observer= factor(obsCovs(umf1)$Observer))

## Fit pcount model ------------------------------------------------------------
##  Estimate observer detection rate (p1 and p2),
##  Estimate abundance, and the effect of habitat

fm1= pcount(~Observer ~HabType,
        umf1,
        K=10,
        engine= c("R","C")[2],
        method= "BFGS", #"Nelder-Mead", #"CG",
        control= list(maxit= 5000),
        se=T)

################################################################################

## Examine results to investigate bug ------------------------------------------

##------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Example of incorrect indexing on predicted detection probability, p1 and p2,
##  following Doug's example shown here:
##  https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/Chisq/unmarked/9AU01DVzel8/hvmU0agNfa4J
##  I do not consider this a "bug", but, rather, "operator error".
expected.counts1= function(fm){

  R = dim(getY(fm@data))[1]

  predict.state= predict(fm, 'state')[,1]
  predict.det= predict(fm, 'det')[,1]

  p1.hat= predict.det[1:R]              ## incorrect indices
  p2.hat= predict.det[(R+1):(R*2)]   ## incorrect indices

  expected= data.frame(y1.hat= predict.state*p1.hat,
                         y2.hat= predict.state*p2.hat)
  return(expected)
}

## Compute X^2 statistic (incorrect) -------------------------------------------
E.ct= expected.counts1(fm1)                ## Expected counts (incorrect)
O.ct= getY(fm1@data)                         ## Observed counts
(Chisq= sum( (E.ct - O.ct)^2 / E.ct) )     ## X^2 (incorrect)
#[1] 32.11523

##------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Correct indexing of p1 and p2, using sequence function to extract
##  p1-hats (odd indices), and p2-hats (even indices)
##  This solves the above example of "operator error"
expected.counts2= function(fm){

  R = dim(getY(fm@data))[1]

  predict.state= predict(fm, 'state')[,1]
  predict.det= predict(fm, 'det')[,1]

  p1.hat= predict.det[seq(1,(2*R),2)]  ## correct indices
  p2.hat= predict.det[seq(2,(2*R),2)]  ## correct indices

  expected= data.frame(y1.hat= predict.state*p1.hat,
                         y2.hat= predict.state*p2.hat)
  return(expected)
}

## Compute X^2 statistic (correct) ---------------------------------------------
E.ct= expected.counts2(fm1)                ## Expected counts (correct)
O.ct= getY(fm1@data)                         ## Observed counts
(Chisq= sum( (E.ct - O.ct)^2 / E.ct) )     ## X^2 (correct)
#[1] 23.47324

##------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Compute expected counts and X^2 using fitted() ------------------------------
## This shows that results from fitted() are equivalent to expected.counts2()
E.ct = fitted(fm1)                                ## Expected counts (correct, again)
O.ct= getY(fm1@data)                       ## Observed counts
(Chisq= sum( (E.ct - O.ct)^2 / E.ct) )   ## X^2 (correct, again)
#[1] 23.47324

################################################################################

## Finally, let's hone in on the appendData "bug", now that we are convinced of
##  the ordering of predicted p's ----------------------------------------------
df.phats= predict(fm1, 'det', appendData=T)      # data.frame of predicted p's
df.Nhats= predict(fm1, 'state', appendData=T)   # data.frame of predicted N's

colnames(df.phats)[1]= "p.hat"
colnames(df.Nhats)[1]= "N.hat"

dim(df.phats)  # data.frame of predicted p's twice as long, with 2 x R rows
dim(df.Nhats)

df.Nhats= cbind(Ni, df.Nhats) # add the true abundance values to Nhat data.frame

## Below, notice i values recycled at row 101, ie, appended data appears
##  as "rbind( fm1@data, fm1@data )", however, predicted p's are ordered
##  p1, p2, p1, p2, etc.
## Given the composition of this data.frame, for each value of i, I might expect
##  a p1 and a p2 estimate, and understand why someone might incorrectly assume
##  that the predicted p's were blocked such that row indices 1:100 are for p1,
##  and 101:200 are for p2.
## However, in each row, we get both counts (y.1, y.2), both observers, and a single
##  prediction of p with no clear association to the y.1 or y.2 column.
> df.phats
         p.hat         SE            lower        upper    y.1 y.2   i HabType Observer.1 Observer.2
1   0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   2   2   1       A      Billy        Bob
2   0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   3   5   2       B      Billy        Bob
3   0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   1   2   3       A      Billy        Bob
4   0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   5   5   4       B      Billy        Bob
5   0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   1   2   5       A      Billy        Bob
6   0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   4   5   6       B      Billy        Bob
...
...
...
99  0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   2   2  99       A      Billy        Bob
100 0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   5   4 100       B      Billy        Bob
101 0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   2   2   1       A      Billy        Bob
102 0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   3   5   2       B      Billy        Bob

## Taking this example a step further, see what happens if we merge
##  df.phats and df.Nhats by the site index, i.  This is tempting, as a step
##  toward computing expected counts by multiplying p-hat by N-hat.

pN.merge= merge(df.Nhats[,c(1,2,8)], df.phats[,c(1,5,6,7,8,9,10)], by="i")

## Below, we see two copies of p1-hat, or two copies of p2-hat,
##  for each site-specific estimate of abundance (N-hat).  What's needed is a
##  single copy of p1-hat, and a single copy of p2-hat, for each site-specific
##  N-hat.  Generating expected counts (p.hat * N.hat) from this merge will
##  yield essentially the same errant result demonstrated with the flawed
##  "expected.counts1()" logic.
> pN.merge
      i   Ni    N.hat     p.hat       y.1 y.2 HabType Observer.1 Observer.2
1     1  2 1.995778 0.8026285   2   2       A      Billy        Bob
2     1  2 1.995778 0.8026285   2   2       A      Billy        Bob
3     2  5 5.031133 0.9620158   3   5       B      Billy        Bob
4     2  5 5.031133 0.9620158   3   5       B      Billy        Bob
5     3  2 1.995778 0.8026285   1   2       A      Billy        Bob
6     3  2 1.995778 0.8026285   1   2       A      Billy        Bob
7     4  5 5.031133 0.9620158   5   5       B      Billy        Bob
8     4  5 5.031133 0.9620158   5   5       B      Billy        Bob
...

I used the term "potential bug" in the subject title for this thread, but
some may not consider this a bug by strict definition.  In deed, the
predict(... "det") function does construct estimates of p that are representative
of the fitted model.  While it is incumbent on the analyst to verify that
"canned" functions work according to their assumptions, I think it is easy to
make the type of errors I have pointed out, as evidenced by the linked discussion.
For that reason, I wanted to highlight my observations on this issue, in case
it saves anybody else some trouble; and maybe the manner of appending data
could be made more "fool proof" (it is Apr 1 afterall!).

One last point for those that have never extracted the observation-covariates from
an unmarked frame:  they are not output in the same format as inputted.  The
ordering of observation-level covariates extracted is what hinted at the ordering
of p-hats returned from the predict function.

> obsCovs(umf1)
    Observer
1      Billy
2        Bob
3      Billy
4        Bob
...
199    Billy
200      Bob

Anyways... I hope this is somewhat helpful.

Best,
Ted

messages.body_plain:
Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology using BUGS and R:
site-structured models for abundance (Workshop)

Instructors: Marc Kéry & Andy Royle, Swiss Ornithological Institute & USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center
Date: 16–18 June 2014
Venue: USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center, Laurel, Maryland
Computers: Bring your own laptop with latest R/unmarked and WinBUGS/OpenBUGS/JAGS
Course fee: USD$450 (normal rate), USD$300 (student rate), 2 wild cards available.

The analysis of abundance and of the dynamic rates governing their change lies at the core of ecology and its applications such as conservation and wildlife management. Metapopulation designs, where repeated measurements of some quantity such as counts or distance measurements are made at a collection of sites, underlie a vast number of studies in ecology and management. Inference about such data is conveniently based on hierarchical models, where one submodel describes the underlying true state of the process (e.g., abundance at a site) and another submodel describes the observation process that connects the true state to the observations.

In recent years, much progress has been made in the development of methods and computer algorithms to fit hierarchical models. In particular, Bayesian statistical analysis and the general-purpose Bayesian software package WinBUGS have opened up entirely new possibilities for ecologists to conduct complex population analyses. On the other hand, the R package unmarked contains a wealth of functions to analyse hierarchical models of abundance in a frequentist mode of inference.

This course introduces key hierarchical models used in the analysis of abundance and its spatial and temporal patterns, and provides both Bayesian and the frequentist methods for their analysis. We use package unmarked in R as well as WinBUGS and JAGS to fit and understand some of the most widely used models for the analysis of animal and plant populations. These include:
- binomial (Royle 2004) and multinomial N-mixture models (e.g., removal, double-observer) for the analysis of distribution and abundance,
- CAR modeling of spatial autocorrelation in abundance
- hierarchical distance sampling models (e.g., Royle et al. 2004, Conn et al. 2012),
- dynamic models of abundance (Royle & Dorazio 2008; Dail & Madsen 2011)

This is an intermediate-level workshop with about 80% spent lecturing and 20% on solving exercises. A working knowledge of modern regression methods (GLMs, mixed models) and preferentially of program R or another programming language is required. messages.body_plain:
Greeting all,

I recently posed a question to Murray Efford, but I'm interested in your opinions.

First, I'll acknowledge a number of different models implemented in unmarked (e.g. gdistsamp) and elsewhere (e.g. staggered-entry models of Kendall et al. 2013 implemented in PRESENCE) allow the separate modeling of detectability (p) from availability for detection (phi) in order to relax assumptions of the given model (e.g. perfection detection at d = 0, closure within a season).

Lacking a general way of estimating phi in an occu or colext model, I'm curious if I'm correct in assuming that I can estimate p as a surrogate for phi in the following scenario (I tried to simplify the example as much as possible):

1. A study has 100 sites, sites are a 1-km squares.
2. Animals can only be detected when they move from vegetated "non-visibility areas" (99% of the 1-km site area) to one small part of a site where they are visible (the "visibility area").
3. Animals are so incredibly conspicuous when in  "visibility areas" that detectability is 100%.
4. A number of factors (e.g. daily weather conditions) influence whether animals are in "non-visibility areas" vs "visibility areas" within a season.
5. Given an animal is present (detected at least once) in a "visibility area", it is typically only detected on 50% of visits, but data from radiomarked animals indicate this animal remained within the 1-km site throughout a season (thus within-season closure).

To summarize:
In this scenario, detectability is essentially perfect, but availability for detection is not, which results in underestimated occupancy (and biases predictions of colonization and extirpation).

In modeling p using survey covariates (such as daily weather), can I assume I'm modeling phi?  Are their pitfalls associated with this assumption?

Thanks for any thoughts.

Giancarlo

hi unmarkers and hello again, Marina,

I believe that a large part of the problems that people have with a package such as unmarked stems from the fact that a linear model must be specified: what do parameters mean, how do I combine the effects of two or more covariates, how can I get predictions (e.g., in a plot of survival probability against some covariate).

These problems have nothing to do with the specific kind of model, but are much more fundamental. They have to do with the linear model, which is the usual way in which we specify effects of discrete or continuous explanatory variables in our analyses. I am convinced that with a better grasp of the "applied fundamentals" of linear models and generalised linear models (only major thing there to understand is the link function) we can get a MUCH better understanding of hierarchical models such as those fit in unmarked. Indeed, half of the power of modern statistical modeling with packages such as MARK, PRESENCE, unmarked or even with the BUGS programming language consists of you being able to specify linear models in a clever way.

I haven't researched about accessible intros of the linear model and GLMs for ecologists. (Probably somebody should write an intro book for ecologists.) However, one of the best that I have ever seen is Evan Cooch's intro to linear models in his Gentle Introduction to Mark (http://www.phidot.org/software/mark/docs/book/, and then choose chapter 6). Of course, for people interested in the models in unmarked, you may have to do some mental translation, for instance, from survival probabilities in a CJS model to occupancy probability in an occupancy model, but the right-hand side of the equation, the linear model, stays the same, regardless of what's on the left-hand side.

Kind regards  --  Marc

messages.subject_clean: treating "availability for detection" as "detectability" in an occu or colext model?
messages.body_plain:
I don't see a problem with this.  Traditional occupancy models assume that availability is random and effectively treat it as constant, so that variation in detection probability (p) can be ascribed to detectability alone.  But you could just as easily assume that detectability was constant and ascribe the variation to availability.  Since you are arguing that detectability is not only constant, but essentially 1, you are in even better shape.  Obviously if the probability is near 1 then variation is absent or inconsequential.

The standard assumption that availability is random can be pretty poor depending on how the scale of your sample site relates to the movement of your focal species and whether attributes that affect occurrence/abundance can also affect behavior.  In my opinion, the distinction between and potential importance of availability vs. detectability is under-appreciated, but I suppose folks have a hard enough time just dealing with detection probability.  Spatial capture-recapture addresses this in a different context, though see Richard and Andy's recent paper for an application to unmarked individuals (Chandler & Royle 2013 Ann. Appl. Stat.).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ted,

unmarked always does things in row-major order. This might be confusing since the R convention is column-major order. I think this explains most of what you are seeing, but I would suggest that you avoid using appendData=TRUE if no new data are provided. I didn't anticipate that anyone would ever do that, so I need to add some code to properly handle that case.

Richard

On Tue, Apr 1, 2014 at 5:51 PM, Ted Jones <salmo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Richard,
>
> Here's a short reproducible example, with some long-winded observations...
>
> ################################################################################
>
> library(unmarked)
> set.seed(81)
>
> # Simulated double-observer survey data
> i= 1:100                 # Site index, 100 sites total
> Ni= rep(c(2,5), 50)      # True abundance at sites, mean lambda alternating between 2 and 5
>
> HabType= rep(c("A","B"), 50) # Habitat type that abundance depends on.
>
> p1= 0.80                 # Detection probability of first observer ("Billy")
> p2= 0.95                 # Detection probability of second observer ("Bob")
>
> Name1= rep("Billy", 100) # Name of first observer
> Name2= rep("Bob", 100)   # Name of second observer
>
> ## Observation-level covariates ------------------------------------------------
> obsCovs= list( Observer= cbind(Name1, Name2) )
>
> ## Counts ----------------------------------------------------------------------
> Count1= rbinom(length(i), Ni, p1)  # Billy's counts
> Count2= rbinom(length(i), Ni, p2)  # Bob's counts
> y= cbind(Count1, Count2) # response formatted for umf
>
> ## Site-level covariates -------------------------------------------------------
> siteCovs= data.frame( i= i,
>                       HabType= as.factor(HabType))
>
> ## Construct the unmarked frame ------------------------------------------------
> umf1= unmarkedFramePCount(y=y, siteCovs=siteCovs, obsCovs=obsCovs)
>
> (obsCovs(umf1)$Observer= factor(obsCovs(umf1)$Observer))
>
> ## Fit pcount model ------------------------------------------------------------
> ##  Estimate observer detection rate (p1 and p2),
> ##  Estimate abundance, and the effect of habitat
>
> fm1= pcount(~Observer ~HabType,
>         umf1,
>         K=10,
>         engine= c("R","C")[2],
>         method= "BFGS", #"Nelder-Mead", #"CG",
>         control= list(maxit= 5000),
>         se=T)
>
> ################################################################################
>
> ## Examine results to investigate bug ------------------------------------------
>
> ##------------------------------------------------------------------------------
> ## Example of incorrect indexing on predicted detection probability, p1 and p2,
> ##  following Doug's example shown here:
> ##  https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/Chisq/unmarked/9AU01DVzel8/hvmU0agNfa4J
> ##  I do not consider this a "bug", but, rather, "operator error".
> expected.counts1= function(fm){
>   R = dim(getY(fm@data))[1]
>
>   predict.state= predict(fm, 'state')[,1]
>   predict.det= predict(fm, 'det')[,1]
>
>   p1.hat= predict.det[1:R]              ## incorrect indices
>   p2.hat= predict.det[(R+1):(R*2)]   ## incorrect indices
>
>   expected= data.frame(y1.hat= predict.state*p1.hat,
>                          y2.hat= predict.state*p2.hat)
>   return(expected)
> }
>
> ## Compute X^2 statistic (incorrect) -------------------------------------------
> E.ct= expected.counts1(fm1)                ## Expected counts (incorrect)
> O.ct= getY(fm1@data)                         ## Observed counts
> (Chisq= sum( (E.ct - O.ct)^2 / E.ct) )     ## X^2 (incorrect)
> #[1] 32.11523
>
> ##------------------------------------------------------------------------------
> ## Correct indexing of p1 and p2, using sequence function to extract
> ##  p1-hats (odd indices), and p2-hats (even indices)
> ##  This solves the above example of "operator error"
> expected.counts2= function(fm){
>   R = dim(getY(fm@data))[1]
>
>   predict.state= predict(fm, 'state')[,1]
>   predict.det= predict(fm, 'det')[,1]
>
>   p1.hat= predict.det[seq(1,(2*R),2)]  ## correct indices
>   p2.hat= predict.det[seq(2,(2*R),2)]  ## correct indices
>
>   expected= data.frame(y1.hat= predict.state*p1.hat,
>                          y2.hat= predict.state*p2.hat)
>   return(expected)
> }
>
> ## Compute X^2 statistic (correct) ---------------------------------------------
> E.ct= expected.counts2(fm1)                ## Expected counts (correct)
> O.ct= getY(fm1@data)                         ## Observed counts
> (Chisq= sum( (E.ct - O.ct)^2 / E.ct) )     ## X^2 (correct)
> #[1] 23.47324
>
> ##------------------------------------------------------------------------------
> ## Compute expected counts and X^2 using fitted() ------------------------------
> ## This shows that results from fitted() are equivalent to expected.counts2()
> E.ct = fitted(fm1)                                ## Expected counts (correct, again)
> O.ct= getY(fm1@data)                       ## Observed counts
> (Chisq= sum( (E.ct - O.ct)^2 / E.ct) )   ## X^2 (correct, again)
> #[1] 23.47324
>
> ################################################################################
>
> ## Finally, let's hone in on the appendData "bug", now that we are convinced of
> ##  the ordering of predicted p's ----------------------------------------------
> df.phats= predict(fm1, 'det', appendData=T)      # data.frame of predicted p's
> df.Nhats= predict(fm1, 'state', appendData=T)   # data.frame of predicted N's
>
> colnames(df.phats)[1]= "p.hat"
> colnames(df.Nhats)[1]= "N.hat"
>
> dim(df.phats)  # data.frame of predicted p's twice as long, with 2 x R rows
> dim(df.Nhats)
>
> df.Nhats= cbind(Ni, df.Nhats) # add the true abundance values to Nhat data.frame
>
> ## Below, notice i values recycled at row 101, ie, appended data appears
> ##  as "rbind( fm1@data, fm1@data )", however, predicted p's are ordered
> ##  p1, p2, p1, p2, etc.
> ## Given the composition of this data.frame, for each value of i, I might expect
> ##  a p1 and a p2 estimate, and understand why someone might incorrectly assume
> ##  that the predicted p's were blocked such that row indices 1:100 are for p1,
> ##  and 101:200 are for p2.
> ## However, in each row, we get both counts (y.1, y.2), both observers, and a single
> ##  prediction of p with no clear association to the y.1 or y.2 column.
> > df.phats
>          p.hat         SE            lower        upper    y.1 y.2   i HabType Observer.1 Observer.2
> 1   0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   2   2   1       A      Billy        Bob
> 2   0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   3   5   2       B      Billy        Bob
> 3   0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   1   2   3       A      Billy        Bob
> 4   0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   5   5   4       B      Billy        Bob
> 5   0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   1   2   5       A      Billy        Bob
> 6   0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   4   5   6       B      Billy        Bob
> ...
> ...
> ...
> 99  0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   2   2  99       A      Billy        Bob
> 100 0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   5   4 100       B      Billy        Bob
> 101 0.8026285 0.02423093 0.7508242 0.8458735   2   2   1       A      Billy        Bob
> 102 0.9620158 0.01731320 0.9091447 0.9846396   3   5   2       B      Billy        Bob
>
> ## Taking this example a step further, see what happens if we merge
> ##  df.phats and df.Nhats by the site index, i.  This is tempting, as a step
> ##  toward computing expected counts by multiplying p-hat by N-hat.
>
> pN.merge= merge(df.Nhats[,c(1,2,8)], df.phats[,c(1,5,6,7,8,9,10)], by="i")
>
> ## Below, we see two copies of p1-hat, or two copies of p2-hat,
> ##  for each site-specific estimate of abundance (N-hat).  What's needed is a
> ##  single copy of p1-hat, and a single copy of p2-hat, for each site-specific
> ##  N-hat.  Generating expected counts (p.hat * N.hat) from this merge will
> ##  yield essentially the same errant result demonstrated with the flawed
> ##  "expected.counts1()" logic.
> > pN.merge
>       i   Ni    N.hat     p.hat       y.1 y.2 HabType Observer.1 Observer.2
> 1     1  2 1.995778 0.8026285   2   2       A      Billy        Bob
> 2     1  2 1.995778 0.8026285   2   2       A      Billy        Bob
> 3     2  5 5.031133 0.9620158   3   5       B      Billy        Bob
> 4     2  5 5.031133 0.9620158   3   5       B      Billy        Bob
> 5     3  2 1.995778 0.8026285   1   2       A      Billy        Bob
> 6     3  2 1.995778 0.8026285   1   2       A      Billy        Bob
> 7     4  5 5.031133 0.9620158   5   5       B      Billy        Bob
> 8     4  5 5.031133 0.9620158   5   5       B      Billy        Bob
> ...
>
> I used the term "potential bug" in the subject title for this thread, but
> some may not consider this a bug by strict definition.  In deed, the
> predict(... "det") function does construct estimates of p that are representative
> of the fitted model.  While it is incumbent on the analyst to verify that
> "canned" functions work according to their assumptions, I think it is easy to

>

>

messages.body_plain:
Dear community, I really hope someone can come up with an idea for me. I'm trying to predict a raster, but one of my input rasters appear to be erroneous. If I ommit it from the prediction it runs fine, but with it included, R will crash.

I've checked projection, extent and cellsize and they all match. It's a factor layer, but so are some of the other predictor rasters. I don't think my code is wrong as I can run the whole thing without this particular raster. I've reclassified it, cut it into smaller pieces, but nothing seems to help. Except that some of the smaller pieces will run with it, but one of them won't. That's why I expect it to have an error somewhere, but don't know what to look for.

Do any of you have an idea as to what I could try to set this raster straight? It looks fine in ArcGIS. All my input rasters are ESRI Grids. It's the fgjord, that's misbehaving.

TIA,
Mette

My code looks like this:
library(Cubist)
library(caret)
library(class)

setwd("D:/dtemp/Texture/ModellingMarch2014")
data<-read.table(file="clay_silt_fsand_Adata.txt", header=T, sep=";")
str(data)####data structure

###########give factor data####
data$georeg<-as.factor(data$georeg)
data$landscape<-as.factor(data$landscape)
data$wetlands<-as.factor(data$wetlands)
data$landuse<-as.factor(data$landuse)
data$geology<-as.factor(data$geology)
data$fgjord<-as.factor(data$fgjord)

names(data)

nc<-ncol(data)
data_predictors<-data[,c(6:nc)]

####make cubist model####
ctrl<- trainControl(method = "LGOCV",repeats=10, number=10,
                    summaryFunction = defaultSummary, selectionFunction = "best")
cubist_model<-train(data[,c(6:nc)],data[,2],method="cubist",trControl=ctrl)
###########package for read rasters###
library(raster)
library(rgdal)

#########read raster file###
aspect<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/aspect")
centallav0<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/centallav0")
dirinsola<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/dirinsola")
elevation<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/elevation")
fgjord<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/fgjord")
flowaccu<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/flowaccu")
geology<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/geology")
georeg<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/georeg")
landscape<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/landscape")
landuse<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/landuse")
midslppos<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/midslppos")
mrvbf<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/mrvbf")
sagawi<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/sagawi")
slpdeg<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/slpdeg")
valldepth<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/valldepth")
vdistchn<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/vdistchn")
wetlands<-raster("D:/dtemp/Texture/Tiles/Tile1/wetlands")

predictors<-c(aspect,centallav0,dirinsola,elevation,fgjord,flowaccu,geology,
              georeg,landscape,landuse,midslppos,
              mrvbf,sagawi,slpdeg,valldepth,vdistchn,wetlands)

var.stack <- stack(predictors)###all input should have same extent and cell size

#Cubist_result ###print the result

capture.output(summary(cubist_model), file = "summary(cubist_model_clayA_tile1).txt")###write results out to text file

system.time(predict(var.stack, cubist_model,
                    filename="D:/dtemp/Texture/ModellingMarch2014/clayA_tile1.img",
                    fun=predict, ext=NULL, const=NULL, index=1, na.rm=TRUE, progress="text",
                    format="HFA", overwrite=TRUE))

Dear Doug,

you want a model where p depends on N or on lambda. I agree that such a model may make sense ecologically under some situations. Also, for birds, for instance, it’s quite possible that individuals sing more when they occur at higher density. Such a model cannot be fitted in unmarked.

A while ago I experimented with such a model of density-dependent detection and fitted it in BUGS. Things seemed to work well for simulated data but when I applied it to real data, I got some nonsensical results and then gave up.

At any case, if you want to pursue this idea you would very probably have to move to BUGS.

Kind regards  --- Marc
